opus-5.5.text:
I don't think the architecture is really the core issue. People sometimes hope that if we just moved away from deep learning to something more interpretable, like symbolic systems or some hybrid approach, the safety problems would go away. And certainly neural networks make things harder in specific ways. They're black boxes, we don't fully understand what they've learned, and we're growing them more than engineering them. So interpretability is a real problem there.

But the impossibility results I'm concerned about are not specific to neural networks. They apply to any sufficiently capable general intelligence. If you have a system that is smarter than you across all domains, it doesn't matter whether it's built out of neurons, logic gates, or something we haven't invented yet. You still can't fully predict what it will do, because if you could, you'd be as smart as it is. You still can't fully explain its decisions to a human in a way the human can verify, because the explanation would have to be compressed to fit our limited capacity. And you still can't guarantee its behavior across an unbounded space of novel situations.

Even a perfectly transparent system, where you can see every line of code, doesn't help you if the code is a billion lines long and doing things you can't comprehend. Transparency isn't understanding. We have fully open-source software today with bugs nobody has found for decades.

So a different architecture might buy us some improvements, maybe better debugging, maybe narrower systems that are easier to test. And I'm actually in favor of that. I think narrow AI, built for specific problems, is something we can make relatively safe. But the moment you're talking about general superintelligence, the problem is fundamentally about the relationship between a less capable agent trying to control a more capable one. Changing the substrate doesn't change that relationship.

r001.rationale: The response says the impossibility results apply to any sufficiently capable general intelligence and are not specific to neural networks.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a very natural hope, and I understand why people have it. Neural networks are black boxes, they're trained rather than designed, we don't understand why they do what they do, so the thought is: if we just switch to something transparent, something symbolic, something we actually engineer line by line, the problems go away. And some of them might. Interpretability would get easier. Maybe you could do formal verification on parts of the system.

But I think the core problems I worry about are not problems with neural networks specifically. They're problems with intelligence. They're problems with controlling something that is smarter than you. If you have a system, whatever the substrate, that is capable of general problem solving at a superhuman level, you still have the question of how do you specify what you want in a way that doesn't have loopholes, how do you verify that it will keep doing that in situations you've never tested, how do you make sure it doesn't modify itself or create successors that don't share your constraints. None of that is architecture-dependent. A perfectly transparent system that is a million times smarter than you is still something you can't really predict, because if you could predict its decisions, you wouldn't need it.

There's also a historical point. People tried the alternatives. Expert systems, logic-based AI, good old-fashioned AI, decades of it. Those approaches had their own failure modes, brittleness, the inability to handle the real world, and crucially they didn't scale to the capabilities we actually care about. The thing that worked was the thing we understand least. That's not an accident. The reason neural networks are hard to interpret is related to why they're powerful. You're compressing enormous complexity into a representation no human designed. If you want a system to handle the complexity of the real world, it probably has to be, internally, at least as complex as that world, and then you're back to not understanding it.

So my honest answer is: a different architecture might make some safety problems easier, maybe meaningfully easier, and I would support research in that direction. But I don't think it removes the fundamental issue, which is that control of a superintelligent agent, by a less intelligent agent, over an indefinite time horizon, may simply not be a solvable problem regardless of what the agent is made of. The hope that we'll find the one architecture where that becomes easy, to me, looks a bit like hoping the problem will go away rather than facing it.

r001.rationale: The response says the core safety problems are not specific to neural networks and are not architecture-dependent.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think the fundamental problem is specific to neural networks. A different architecture might be easier to interpret, easier to verify, and that would be useful. But you still have to specify what you want the system to do, and show that it will continue doing that when it learns, modifies itself, or encounters situations you didn’t anticipate.

With a narrowly constrained system, you can prove certain properties under certain assumptions. The difficulty is extending those guarantees to a general intelligence operating in the real world. Your proof may be correct, but your assumptions about the world may not be.

So I’m open to someone proposing an architecture that changes the safety argument. But “it’s not a neural network” is not, by itself, a safety guarantee. You have to explain which problem it solves and why that solution continues to hold as the system becomes more capable.

r001.rationale: The response says the fundamental problem is not specific to neural networks and that merely using a different architecture does not guarantee safety.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think the fundamental problem is specific to neural networks. A different architecture might be easier to inspect or verify, and that could help with particular safety problems. But you still have to explain why a system more intelligent than you will remain under your control as it encounters situations you didn’t anticipate.

You can prove properties of a program under certain assumptions. The difficulty is making sure those assumptions capture the real world, and that the property you proved is actually what you wanted. A system can satisfy a formal specification and still produce an outcome we consider disastrous because the specification was incomplete.

So I’m open to alternative architectures. But changing the architecture by itself is not a solution. You need a convincing argument for safety that applies to the system’s capabilities and behavior.

r001.rationale: The response says the fundamental problem is not specific to neural networks and that changing architecture alone does not solve it.
